concept.name: Authorized participant
concept.definition: An authorized participant (AP) is a financial institution — typically a large broker-dealer — that enters into a contractual relationship with an exchange-traded fund (ETF) to buy and redeem creation units of ETF shares directly with the fund. APs are the only parties allowed to create or redeem ETF shares in the primary market, usually in large blocks (creation units) and often in kind.
concept.intuition: An AP is the ETF's wholesale door: ordinary investors trade existing ETF shares with each other, but only APs can exchange a basket of underlying securities for new ETF shares (or vice versa) directly with the fund.
concept.mechanics: When ETF demand exceeds supply, the AP assembles the fund's designated basket of securities, delivers it to the ETF, and receives a creation unit (commonly tens of thousands of shares) to sell on the exchange; the process reverses for redemptions. This creation/redemption arbitrage is the mechanism that keeps an ETF's market price close to the value of its underlying holdings.
concept.failure_modes: If APs step back (balance-sheet constraints, stressed or illiquid underlying markets), creation/redemption weakens and ETF prices can trade at persistent premiums or discounts to net asset value. In-kind baskets can also become hard to source in stressed bond or commodity markets.
concept.misconceptions: Retail investors cannot create or redeem ETF shares — they trade only in the secondary market. An AP's role is a contractual privilege, not a guarantee that it will always provide liquidity or that the ETF can never deviate from NAV.
concept.example: An equity ETF trades at a premium to its basket; an AP buys the underlying stocks, delivers them to the fund for a 50,000-share creation unit, and sells the new ETF shares into the market, closing the premium.
